narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score of 22 was by far the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. This score sits far below the average of 37 among students who were admitted, signaling that the model saw your test performance as a significant barrier to passing the bar.

Next, your family income bracket of upper-middle class worked mildly in your favor, slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure. However, this positive effect was too small to offset the other factors.

Your first-year grades, which placed you in the third decile of your class, also provided a small positive nudge toward passing. Yet this contribution was modest and again could not overcome the dominant negative signal from your LSAT performance.

In short, the combination of a low LSAT score with only average early academic standing led the model to conclude you were more likely than not to fail the bar exam, making admission too risky.

What you should do next is focus on substantially improving your LSAT score through targeted preparation, while also strengthening your academic record in the coming year. Retaking the test with a stronger result would be the most direct way to change future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
